# NexaCore API Engineering Standards  
**Document ID:** NC-ENG-API-2026-08
**Version:** 5.0
**Effective:** 01 Aug 2026
**Owner:** Platform Engineering
**Status:** Internal / Controlled
**Data classification:** Internal  
> This document is synthetic private company data created for RAG evaluation. It is not sourced from a real company.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards

chunks.content:
## 1. API Design Baseline  
NexaCore APIs use HTTP semantics consistently and expose machine-readable contracts.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 1. API Design Baseline

chunks.content:
### 1.1 Standard resource conventions  
| Item | Standard |
|---|---|
| Base path | `/api/v1` |
| JSON media type | `application/json` |
| Authentication | OAuth2/JWT depending on service |
| Request ID | `X-Request-ID` |
| Trace ID | `X-Trace-ID` |
| Maximum page size | 100 |
| Default page size | 25 |
| Maximum request body | 2 MB unless service exception |
| Default timeout | 30 seconds |
| Maximum synchronous timeout | 60 seconds |  
Resource names are plural nouns: `/users`, `/projects`, `/invoices`.  
Avoid verbs in resource paths except for explicitly modeled actions such as `/password-reset` or `/token`.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 1. API Design Baseline > 1.1 Standard resource conventions

chunks.content:
## 2. HTTP Status Standards  
| Situation | Status |
|---|---:|
| Successful read | 200 |
| Resource created | 201 |
| Accepted asynchronous operation | 202 |
| Successful delete with no body | 204 |
| Invalid request syntax/validation | 400 |
| Missing/invalid authentication | 401 |
| Authenticated but not authorized | 403 |
| Resource not found | 404 |
| Conflict / duplicate state | 409 |
| Rate limit exceeded | 429 |
| Unexpected server failure | 500 |
| Temporary upstream dependency failure | 503 |  
A successful API must not return `200` for a failed business operation merely because the HTTP request reached the server.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 2. HTTP Status Standards

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 3. Error Contract

chunks.content:
### 3.1 Error-code rules  
- Codes are uppercase `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`.
- Codes are stable identifiers; clients should not parse the human message.
- Do not expose database exception messages.
- Validation errors should identify the field where possible.
- Security-sensitive errors should not reveal whether a protected resource exists.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 3. Error Contract > 3.1 Error-code rules

chunks.content:
## 4. Pagination  
Collection endpoints must paginate when expected result volume can exceed 100 records.  
Preferred response:  
```json
{
"data": [],
"pagination": {
"page": 1,
"page_size": 25,
"total": 413,
"has_next": true
}
}
```  
For high-volume or distributed data, cursor pagination may be used:  
```json
{
"data": [],
"next_cursor": "eyJvZmZzZXQiOjI1fQ=="
}
```  
Cursor values must be opaque to clients.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 4. Pagination

chunks.content:
## 5. Filtering, Sorting and Search  
Supported query parameters should be explicitly documented.  
Example:  
`GET /api/v1/orders?status=OPEN&sort=-created_at&page_size=25`  
Rules:  
1. Do not expose arbitrary database field expressions.
2. Allow-list sortable fields.
3. Validate enum values.
4. Normalize date/time inputs to ISO 8601.
5. Define whether filtering is case-sensitive.
6. Search endpoints should define maximum query length.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 5. Filtering, Sorting and Search

chunks.content:
## 6. Idempotency  
POST requests that create financial, provisioning or other non-repeatable side effects should support an idempotency key.  
Header:  
`Idempotency-Key: 7d9d7e1e-...`  
The server should return the original result for a repeated key where the request body is equivalent.  
Recommended retention for payment/provisioning operations: **24 hours minimum**.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 6. Idempotency

chunks.content:
## 7. Authentication and Authorization  
Authentication proves identity; authorization determines access.  
Required controls:  
- Validate token issuer, audience, expiry and signature.
- Enforce authorization at the service/resource boundary.
- Never trust a user-provided `user_id` merely because it appears in the URL.
- Administrative endpoints require explicit role/permission checks.
- Service-to-service credentials must use managed identity or approved secret storage.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 7. Authentication and Authorization

chunks.content:
## 8. Rate Limiting  
Default platform limits:  
| Consumer type | Sustained rate | Burst |
|---|---:|---:|
| Standard user | 60 req/min | 20 |
| Service client | 300 req/min | 100 |
| Internal batch client | 600 req/min | 200 |
| Authentication endpoints | 10 req/min/IP | 5 |  
Rate-limit responses use HTTP `429` and should include `Retry-After` when practical.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 8. Rate Limiting

chunks.content:
## 9. Versioning and Compatibility  
The public API major version is represented in the path, e.g. `/api/v1`.  
Breaking changes include:  
- Removing a field.
- Changing a field's type.
- Making an optional field mandatory.
- Changing semantic meaning.
- Removing an endpoint.  
Non-breaking additions should remain backward compatible.  
A deprecated endpoint should normally receive at least **90 days** of notice before removal unless security or legal requirements require faster action.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 9. Versioning and Compatibility

chunks.content:
## 10. Time and Date Rules  
- Store timestamps in UTC.
- APIs should return ISO 8601 timestamps with timezone information.
- Business-local dates must be represented as dates rather than midnight UTC timestamps.
- Never infer a user's timezone from browser locale alone when financial or scheduling correctness matters.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 10. Time and Date Rules

chunks.content:
## 11. API Performance Targets  
| API class | Target |
|---|---:|
| Simple read | p95 < 300 ms |
| Normal read/write | p95 < 500 ms |
| Complex query | p95 < 800 ms |
| Synchronous external workflow | p95 < 2 s |
| Absolute synchronous timeout | 60 s |  
A sustained p95 regression greater than 20% requires investigation.

metadata.title: Api Standards
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Api Standards > NexaCore API Engineering Standards > 11. API Performance Targets

chunks.content:
## 12. Documentation Requirements  
Every production API must document:  
- Purpose and ownership
- Authentication
- Endpoint list
- Request/response schemas
- Error codes
- Rate limits
- Pagination
- Examples
- Deprecation status
- Operational dependencies  
**Review cadence:** quarterly.
**Current owner:** Platform Architecture Council.

- Data Architecture
- Transactional workloads use relational storage where consistency and referential integrity are primary requirements.
- Document-oriented storage is used for flexible metadata and selected workflow records.
- Object storage contains large immutable artifacts; database rows retain metadata and references.
- Analytics workloads consume curated datasets rather than directly querying operational databases.
- Sensitive data is classified and access-controlled at the application and storage layers.

## Slide 6: Slide 6  
- Event-Driven Processing
- Asynchronous workflows use domain events to decouple producers from consumers.
- Events contain event_id, event_type, occurred_at, producer, schema_version and payload.
- Consumers must be idempotent because delivery may be retried.
- Dead-letter queues are monitored and reviewed at least daily for Tier-1 event streams.
- Schema changes must preserve consumer compatibility or use a new event version.
- NexaCore Architecture | Internal

- API and Integration Layer
- External integrations terminate through approved integration services rather than allowing arbitrary outbound calls from domain services.
- Outbound calls use timeouts, retry policies and circuit-breaking where appropriate.
- Default retry policy: maximum 3 attempts with exponential backoff for retry-safe operations.
- Authentication secrets are stored in managed secret storage; credentials are never embedded in code.
- Partner integrations must document rate limits, failure behavior and support ownership.
- NexaCore Architecture | Internal

- Tier-1 recovery target: RTO 60 minutes; RPO 15 minutes.

- Metrics cover traffic, errors, latency and saturation.
- Distributed traces connect gateway requests to downstream service calls where instrumentation is available.

- Security Boundaries
- Identity is centralized; services validate authorization for their owned resources.
- Production administrative access is privileged, logged and reviewed.
- Network segmentation separates public ingress, application workloads, data services and management paths.
- Secrets are retrieved at runtime from approved secret-management infrastructure.
- Restricted data must not be copied into development environments without approved masking or synthetic replacement.

- Deployment Architecture
- CI produces a versioned artifact tied to a source commit.
- Staging is the final production-like validation environment.
- Production rollout uses controlled promotion, with canary or phased deployment for Tier-1 services where supported.
- Rollback is preferred when the previous artifact is safe and compatible; irreversible migrations require forward-fix planning.
- Post-deployment smoke tests verify critical paths before the release is considered complete.

## **1. Deployment Model**  
NexaCore uses an environment-separated delivery model: Development → Test → Staging → Production. Promotion is controlled by CI/CD policies rather than manual source copying.

|---|---|---|---|
|Development|Feature development|Synthetic / masked|Developer|
|Test|Automated integration testing|Synthetic|CI|
|Staging|Production-like validation|Masked / approved test|Release owner|
|Production|Customer workloads|Live|Release owner + controls|

- Standard production releases are scheduled Tuesday–Thursday during approved release windows.  
- Friday production releases require explicit engineering manager approval unless they are emergency/security fixes.  
- Tier-1 services require a named release owner and on-call engineer.  
- Production deployment windows are normally 11:00–16:00 IST for standard changes.

### **3.1 Pre-release checklist**  
- Confirm change ticket and owner.  
- Review automated test results and deployment diff.  
- Verify database migration compatibility.  
- Confirm monitoring dashboards and alerts.  
- Confirm rollback or forward-fix plan.  
- Check on-call coverage.  
- Communicate customer-impacting maintenance where required.

### **4.1 Database migration rules**  
- Prefer backward-compatible expand/contract migrations.  
- Large backfills must be throttled and observable.  
- Migration duration must be estimated before production.  
- Destructive operations require explicit approval and verified backup/restore readiness.  
- Application deployment should not depend on a migration completing instantaneously.

### **5.1 Rollback decision**  
Rollback is preferred when the deployed change is the clear cause of customer impact and the previous artifact remains safe. Forward-fix is preferred when rollback would create data incompatibility or the incident is caused by an irreversible migration.

# 1. Engineering Operating Principles  
Engineering teams are expected to optimize for correctness, maintainability, security and operational reliability rather than short-term code volume. Every production change must have an identifiable owner and an auditable path from requirement to deployment.

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 1. Engineering Operating Principles

chunks.content:
## 1.1 Quality priorities  
| Priority | Expected behavior | Measurement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Correctness | Tests cover business-critical paths | Critical path test coverage ≥ 85% |
| Reliability | Services expose health/readiness signals | SLO defined for production services |
| Security | Secrets and privileged operations use approved controls | Zero hard-coded production secrets |
| Maintainability | Code follows repository conventions | Review checklist + static analysis |
| Observability | Failures produce actionable telemetry | Logs + metrics + traces where applicable |

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 1. Engineering Operating Principles > 1.1 Quality priorities

chunks.content:
## 1.2 Repository standards  
- Every production repository must have an owner, README, license/notice file where required, dependency manifest and CI configuration.  
- Default branches are protected; direct pushes to protected production branches are prohibited.  
- Commit messages should identify the intent of a change. Squashed merge commits should reference the ticket or change request.  
- Repository secrets must never be committed, including local development credentials copied into configuration files.  
- Generated artifacts should be separated from source code and must not be committed unless the repository explicitly requires them.

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 1. Engineering Operating Principles > 1.2 Repository standards

chunks.content:
## 1.3 Definition of done  
A change is considered complete only when implementation, tests, review, documentation, monitoring impact and deployment notes are addressed. For customer-impacting changes, rollback or mitigation steps must be documented before production approval.

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 1. Engineering Operating Principles > 1.3 Definition of done

# 2. Code Review and Branching  
## 2.1 Branch naming  
| Type | Pattern | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

## 2.2 Review requirements  
- Normal production changes require at least 1 qualified reviewer.  
- Changes to authentication, authorization, secrets, payment logic or data-retention controls require 2 reviewers, including a domain owner where assigned.  
- Database migrations that can lock or rewrite large tables require an explicit migration plan and rollback/forward-fix strategy.  
- A reviewer should reject a change when requirements are unclear, tests are insufficient, security impact is unexplained, or operational ownership is missing.  
- Large pull requests above 800 changed lines should normally be split unless the change is generated, mechanical or migration-driven.

| PR class | Target first review | Escalation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Routine | Within 1 business day | Team lead after 2 days |
| High priority | Within 4 working hours | Engineering manager after 8 hours |
| Hotfix | Within 30 minutes | On-call lead |
| Security remediation | Within 2 working hours | Security engineering |

## 2.4 Testing expectations  
Unit tests should validate deterministic business logic. Integration tests should cover service boundaries and persistence behavior. End-to-end tests should be reserved for critical user journeys because they carry higher runtime and maintenance cost.

# 3. API, Data and Dependency Practices  
## 3.1 API implementation  
- API contracts must define authentication, request validation, response schema and error behavior.  
- Breaking changes require versioning or an approved compatibility migration.  
- Endpoints should reject unknown or invalid input rather than silently coercing unsafe values.  
- Pagination is required for collections that can exceed 100 records under expected production volume.  
- Request IDs must be propagated across service calls when supported by the platform.

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 3. API, Data and Dependency Practices > 3.1 API implementation

chunks.content:
## 3.2 Database changes  
| Change type | Required control | Default deployment pattern |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Add nullable column | Schema review | Expand → deploy → backfill |
| Add index | Query impact review | Online/low-lock method where supported |
| Rename column | Compatibility plan | Dual-read/write → migrate → remove |
| Delete column | Usage evidence | Deprecate → verify → remove |
| Large backfill | Capacity estimate | Throttled batches + monitoring |

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 3. API, Data and Dependency Practices > 3.2 Database changes

chunks.content:
## 3.3 Dependency management  
- Dependencies must use approved registries and lock files where the ecosystem supports them.  
- Critical vulnerabilities must be triaged within 24 hours of confirmed production exposure.  
- Major dependency upgrades require compatibility testing and release notes review.  
- Unused dependencies should be removed during quarterly repository hygiene reviews.

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 3. API, Data and Dependency Practices > 3.3 Dependency management

chunks.content:
## 3.4 Configuration  
Configuration should be externalized by environment. Local defaults must not accidentally point to production services. Production configuration changes should be auditable and should not require source-code modification unless the platform design explicitly requires it.

# 4. Observability, Performance and Reliability  
## 4.1 Standard telemetry  
| Signal | Minimum requirement | Retention target |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Application logs | Structured JSON + request/correlation ID | 30 days |
| Metrics | Latency, errors, throughput, saturation | 90 days |
| Traces | Critical distributed paths | 14 days |
| Audit events | Security-sensitive actions | 365 days |

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 4. Observability, Performance and Reliability > 4.1 Standard telemetry

chunks.content:
## 4.2 Performance budgets  
- Interactive API endpoints should target p95 latency below 500 ms for normal reads and below 800 ms for normal writes unless the contract specifies otherwise.  
- Background jobs must expose queue age and processing duration.  
- Services should define a resource saturation threshold before production launch; 80% sustained CPU or memory is a common review trigger, not a universal limit.  
- Performance regressions above 20% on a critical endpoint require investigation before release unless the change is explicitly accepted.

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 4. Observability, Performance and Reliability > 4.2 Performance budgets

chunks.content:
## 4.3 Reliability targets  
Production services must document an SLO appropriate to business criticality. The current platform reference uses 99.9% monthly availability for Tier-1 APIs, 99.5% for Tier-2 services and best-effort targets for internal development tools.

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 4. Observability, Performance and Reliability > 4.3 Reliability targets

chunks.content:
## 4.4 Incident learning  
- Incidents affecting customers or production data require a written post-incident review.  
- The review should identify timeline, impact, detection, contributing factors, corrective actions and owners.  
- Corrective actions should have target dates; recurring incidents are reviewed during the monthly reliability meeting.

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 4. Observability, Performance and Reliability > 4.4 Incident learning

chunks.content:
# 5. Security and Secure Development  
## 5.1 Secure coding controls  
- Validate input at the application boundary and enforce authorization at the resource boundary.  
- Do not log passwords, access tokens, session cookies, API keys or full payment-card information.  
- Use parameterized queries or approved ORM mechanisms instead of string-built SQL.  
- Cryptographic operations must use approved platform libraries; custom cryptography is prohibited.  
- Production secrets must be stored in the approved secret-management system.

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 5. Security and Secure Development > 5.1 Secure coding controls

chunks.content:
## 5.2 Security severity targets  
| Severity | Initial response | Target remediation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Critical | ≤ 1 hour | ≤ 24 hours |
| High | ≤ 4 hours | ≤ 7 calendar days |
| Medium | ≤ 2 business days | ≤ 30 calendar days |
| Low | ≤ 5 business days | ≤ 90 calendar days |

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 5. Security and Secure Development > 5.2 Security severity targets

chunks.content:
## 5.3 Access control  
Engineering access follows least privilege. Production access is role-based, time-bounded where supported and logged. Developers should use non-production environments for debugging unless an approved production diagnostic procedure exists.

metadata.title: Engineering Guidelines
metadata.breadcrumbs: engineering > Engineering Guidelines > 5. Security and Secure Development > 5.3 Access control

chunks.content:
## 5.4 Release gates  
- CI must pass before merge.  
- Required security scans must pass or have an approved exception.  
- Database migrations must complete successfully in the deployment sequence.  
- Smoke tests must pass after production rollout.

## **1. Purpose, Scope and Expense Principles**  
This policy defines which business expenses NexaCore may reimburse, who approves them, what evidence is required, and how Finance records and audits employee spending. The values below are synthetic private-company data created for RAG evaluation.

metadata.title: Expense Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: finance > Expense Policy > **NexaCore Expense Policy** > **1. Purpose, Scope and Expense Principles**

chunks.content:
### **1.1 Core rules**  
- Expenses must have a clear business purpose and must be incurred while performing an approved company activity.  
- Employees should use corporate purchasing channels where a company account, purchase order or approved vendor process exists.  
- Personal spending is reimbursable only where the expense is eligible and the employee follows the reimbursement workflow.  
- Receipts are required for individual expenses above INR 1,000 and for all categories designated as controlled spend.  
- An expense must not be split into multiple transactions to avoid an approval threshold.

|---|---|---|

|INR 50,001–2,00,000|Function head|Finance review|

# 1. Reimbursement Lifecycle

- The formal month-3 review identifies whether expectations are on track, at risk or materially below role requirements.  
- The month-6 decision is recorded as confirmed, extended or not confirmed, subject to applicable employment terms.  
- Probation extensions require People Operations review and a written development plan with a maximum initial extension of 3 months.

- Customer or partner commitments must not be communicated as confirmed unless the responsible function has accepted the commitment.

# Remote Work Policy  
NexaCore Remote Work Policy  
Policy ID: NC-HR-RW-2026-08 | Version 3.1 | Effective: 01 Aug 2026 | Owner: People Operations  
This document is synthetic internal company data created for RAG evaluation. It is not a real company's policy.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > Remote Work Policy

chunks.content:
# 1. Scope and Operating Model  
NexaCore uses a role-based hybrid model rather than a universal remote entitlement. The approved work mode is stored in the HRIS and reviewed when employees change roles, teams or locations.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 1. Scope and Operating Model

chunks.content:
## 1.1 Work modes  
| Mode | Default office days | Remote days | Typical eligibility |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Office | 5 | 0 | Lab, infrastructure and designated operational roles |
| Hybrid | 3 | 2 | Most engineering, product, finance and corporate roles |
| Remote | 0–1 | 4–5 | Approved roles with low physical dependency |

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 1. Scope and Operating Model > 1.1 Work modes

chunks.content:
## 1.2 Core hours and availability  
- Core collaboration hours are 10:00–16:00 IST unless a roster states otherwise.  
- Remote employees must maintain a reliable connection during scheduled work hours and attend required meetings.  
- A remote arrangement does not change the employee's expected output, security responsibilities or response commitments.  
- Teams may establish fixed overlap windows where customer, release or support requirements justify them.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 1. Scope and Operating Model > 1.2 Core hours and availability

chunks.content:
## 1.3 Work location  
The employee's approved remote location is recorded at city/state level. Working from another city for more than 5 consecutive business days requires manager approval; cross-state working may require People Operations review.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 1. Scope and Operating Model > 1.3 Work location

chunks.content:
# 2. Eligibility and Approval Workflow  
## 2.1 Eligibility scorecard  
| Criterion | Weight | Pass condition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Role physical dependency | 30% | No mandatory daily physical dependency |
| Security/data sensitivity | 20% | Role can operate under remote security controls |
| Customer coverage | 15% | Customer commitments remain covered |
| Performance history | 20% | No active performance improvement plan |
| Team operating fit | 15% | Manager confirms coverage and collaboration |  
An eligibility assessment is a management control, not an automatic entitlement. A role may be remote-capable while a specific employee is temporarily required to work from office for operational reasons.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 2. Eligibility and Approval Workflow > 2.1 Eligibility scorecard

chunks.content:
## 2.2 Approval workflow  
- Employee submits the remote-work request in the HRIS.  
- Manager reviews role coverage, performance, collaboration and schedule impact within 3 business days.  
- Function head approval is required for permanent remote status and for exceptions longer than 30 days.  
- People Operations updates the HRIS after approval; email approval alone does not change the authoritative work-mode record.  
- IT/Security review is required when the proposed arrangement introduces unusual device, network or data-handling risk.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 2. Eligibility and Approval Workflow > 2.2 Approval workflow

chunks.content:
## 2.3 Temporary remote exception  
A manager may approve up to 10 business days of temporary remote work for an employee whose standard mode is Office or Hybrid. More than 10 days requires function-head approval.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 2. Eligibility and Approval Workflow > 2.3 Temporary remote exception

chunks.content:
# 3. Equipment, Workspace and Connectivity  
## 3.1 Standard equipment allocation  
| Item | Standard issue | Replacement trigger |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Laptop | 1 managed device | Lifecycle / failure |
| External monitor | 1 for eligible roles | Failure / approved ergonomic need |
| Headset | 1 | Failure |
| Keyboard + mouse | 1 set | Failure / ergonomic need |
| Security key | 1 where role requires MFA hardware | Loss / failure |

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 3. Equipment, Workspace and Connectivity > 3.1 Standard equipment allocation

chunks.content:
## 3.2 Connectivity  
- Employees are expected to maintain a stable internet connection sufficient for video meetings and approved work systems.  
- For recurring outages, employees should notify their manager and use an approved office or backup location where feasible.  
- Company work must not be performed over untrusted public Wi-Fi without the approved VPN/security controls.  
- Personal hotspots may be used temporarily where approved, but confidential data must remain inside approved systems.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 3. Equipment, Workspace and Connectivity > 3.2 Connectivity

chunks.content:
## 3.3 Home workspace  
The employee should maintain a private work area where screens, documents and conversations cannot be viewed or overheard by unauthorized persons. Physical company records should not be stored in shared household spaces.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 3. Equipment, Workspace and Connectivity > 3.3 Home workspace

chunks.content:
## 3.4 Asset incidents  
Loss or suspected theft of a company device must be reported to IT/Security immediately and no later than 30 minutes after discovery where reasonably possible. Delayed reporting can increase security exposure.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 3. Equipment, Workspace and Connectivity > 3.4 Asset incidents

chunks.content:
# 4. Security Controls for Remote Work  
## 4.1 Authentication  
- Multi-factor authentication is mandatory for corporate identity systems.  
- Employees must not share passwords, session tokens, recovery codes or security keys.  
- Screens must lock after the configured inactivity period; employees should manually lock before leaving the workspace.  
- Privileged administrative access must use the approved privileged-access workflow.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 4. Security Controls for Remote Work > 4.1 Authentication

chunks.content:
## 4.2 Data handling  
| Data class | Remote handling | Storage rule |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Public | Allowed | Approved company systems |
| Internal | Allowed | Approved company systems only |
| Confidential | Controlled | Managed device + approved storage |
| Restricted | Case-specific | Additional controls / approval |

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 4. Security Controls for Remote Work > 4.2 Data handling

chunks.content:
## 4.3 Meetings and calls  
Confidential customer, HR, security or financial discussions must be conducted in a private environment. Recording is prohibited unless the meeting owner has confirmed the required notice/approval and the recording is stored in an approved system.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 4. Security Controls for Remote Work > 4.3 Meetings and calls

chunks.content:
## 4.4 Printing  
Printing confidential or restricted information at home should be avoided. If business necessity requires it, documents must be secured and destroyed using an approved method when no longer required.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 4. Security Controls for Remote Work > 4.4 Printing

chunks.content:
# 5. Productivity, Collaboration and Travel  
## 5.1 Collaboration expectations  
- Employees should keep calendars accurate and mark availability for core collaboration hours.  
- Project status should be updated at the cadence defined by the team, typically at least twice per week.  
- A missed meeting due to connectivity or other remote-work disruption should be communicated through the team channel.  
- Remote status cannot be used as a reason to defer customer-critical or release-critical work without manager agreement.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 5. Productivity, Collaboration and Travel > 5.1 Collaboration expectations

chunks.content:
## 5.2 Travel while working remotely  
Working while travelling is permitted only when the destination is within an approved jurisdiction and the employee can maintain security and work-hour obligations. International work from outside India requires prior People Operations and tax/legal review.

metadata.title: Remote Work Policy
metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 5. Productivity, Collaboration and Travel > 5.2 Travel while working remotely

chunks.content:
## 5.3 Remote-work performance indicators  
| Indicator | Target / control |
| :--- | :--- |
| Core-hours attendance | ≥ 90% of scheduled core-hour obligations, excluding approved leave |
| Required meeting attendance | As defined by team; customer meetings are mandatory unless delegated |
| Status updates | Minimum 2 per week for active project assignments |
| Security training | 100% completion by assigned deadline |

metadata.breadcrumbs: hr > Remote Work Policy > 5. Productivity, Collaboration and Travel > 5.3 Remote-work performance indicators

- Termination rights and notice periods must be recorded in the vendor record.

## 4.3 Corrective action  
- Document issue and evidence.  
- Agree corrective action and due date.  
- Assign supplier and internal owners.  
- Track weekly for critical issues.  
- Escalate unresolved high-risk issues to Procurement Head.  
- Consider alternate supplier if remediation fails.

# 5. Renewal and Offboarding  
## 5.1 Renewal timeline  
- 120 days before expiry: confirm business need and spend.  
- 90 days: performance and risk review.  
- 60 days: commercial negotiation / alternatives.  
- 30 days: final approval and contract execution.  
- Post-renewal: update vendor record and repository.

metadata.title: Vendor Management
metadata.breadcrumbs: operations > Vendor Management > 5. Renewal and Offboarding > 5.1 Renewal timeline

## 5.2 Offboarding checklist  
- Revoke system access.  
- Recover company assets where applicable.  
- Confirm data return/deletion obligations.  
- Stop purchase orders.  
- Close open invoices.  
- Archive contract and performance record.  
- Document termination reason.

Discounts are commercial tools, not default pricing. Sales must establish business justification and protect minimum economics before requesting a concession.

| >5–10% | Request | Approve | Visibility | — |

- Splitting an order to avoid a discount threshold.  
- Backdating an approval.  
- Describing a discount as a temporary exception when it is intended as recurring pricing.  
- Offering unapproved free services or implementation credits.  
- Using a personal promise to compensate for a commercial concession.

## 1. Access Control Model  
NexaCore uses role-based access control (RBAC) with attribute checks where resource context requires them. Access follows **least privilege**, **need to know**, and **separation of duties**.

metadata.title: Access Control
metadata.breadcrumbs: security > Access Control > NexaCore Access Control Standard > 1. Access Control Model

chunks.content:
### 1.1 Core principles  
1. Every production permission must map to a business or operational requirement.
2. Access should be granted to roles/groups rather than directly to individuals when the platform supports groups.
3. Privileged access requires MFA and enhanced logging.
4. Access reviews must verify actual need, not merely manager ownership.
5. Dormant accounts and stale permissions must be removed or disabled.

metadata.title: Access Control
metadata.breadcrumbs: security > Access Control > NexaCore Access Control Standard > 1. Access Control Model > 1.1 Core principles

| Role | Typical scope | Privilege |

| Employee | Corporate applications | Standard |
| Manager | Team reporting/workflows | Elevated business |
| Application Admin | Specific application | Privileged |
| Platform Engineer | Infrastructure services | Privileged |
| Security Analyst | Security systems | Privileged |
| Finance Admin | Finance systems | Restricted business |
| Break-glass Admin | Emergency production recovery | Emergency privileged |

## 3. Joiner / Mover / Leaver Controls  
### Joiner  
HR creates the identity record. Standard access is provisioned based on department and role. Additional access requires application-owner approval.

metadata.title: Access Control
metadata.breadcrumbs: security > Access Control > NexaCore Access Control Standard > 3. Joiner / Mover / Leaver Controls > Joiner

chunks.content:

When an employee changes department or role, previous access must be reviewed rather than assuming the old role remains valid.  
Target: **4 business hours** for standard role changes.

metadata.title: Access Control
metadata.breadcrumbs: security > Access Control > NexaCore Access Control Standard > 3. Joiner / Mover / Leaver Controls > Mover

chunks.content:

Access is disabled according to HR termination timing. Immediate termination/security-risk cases require immediate revocation after notification.

## 4. Privileged Access  
Privileged accounts must:  
- Use MFA.
- Use named identities.
- Avoid shared credentials.
- Be logged.
- Have an owner.
- Be reviewed quarterly.
- Use temporary elevation where supported.

metadata.breadcrumbs: security > Access Control > NexaCore Access Control Standard > 4. Privileged Access > 4.1 Privileged session controls

## 5. Production Access  
Production access is divided into:  
- Read-only diagnostic access
- Operational write access
- Deployment access
- Security administration
- Database administration  
A developer does not automatically receive production database write access merely because they can deploy application code.

| Access type | Requester | Approver |

| Standard application | Employee | Manager + application owner |
| Sensitive application | Employee | Manager + data/application owner |
| Production read | Engineer | Manager + service owner |
| Production write | Engineer | Service owner + security/authorized approver |
| Privileged admin | Engineer/Admin | Manager + system owner |

- Active users

Accounts inactive for **45 days** are candidates for review. Privileged accounts inactive for **30 days** require explicit validation.

## 8. Service Accounts  
Every service account must have:  
- Unique owner
- Business purpose
- System scope
- Credential rotation method
- Expiry/review date
- Non-human identity classification  
Service accounts should not be used for interactive human login.

## 9. Break-Glass Access  
Break-glass access is restricted to emergency recovery. It must:  
1. Be used only when normal access is unavailable or insufficient.
2. Generate an audit record.
3. Be reviewed within 1 business day.
4. Have credentials protected separately from normal administration.
5. Be rotated after use where the credential model requires it.

============================================================

- Confirmed compromise of a single non-critical endpoint.
- Suspicious activity with limited confirmed impact.
- Policy violation with potential security consequences.
Target acknowledgement: 1 hour.  
SEV-4 LOW
Examples:
- Low-risk policy deviation.
- Benign alert requiring investigation.
